nameStory: The southern red-backed vole gets its name from the distinctive rusty-red stripe that runs down its back like a natural racing stripe. This colorful marking makes it stand out from other small rodents in New England's forests. It's also called Gapper's red-backed vole, named after Anthony Gapper, a 19th-century naturalist who studied Canadian wildlife.
description: The southern red-backed vole is a small, mouse-sized rodent about the length of your thumb with a chestnut-red stripe running down its back. Unlike house mice, it has a chunky, compact body with short legs and a relatively short tail. These little forest dwellers have rich brown fur on their sides that contrasts beautifully with their red backs and grayish bellies. They're active year-round and are one of the most common small mammals in New England's woodlands.

idTips.label: Fur
idTips.description: Look for the distinctive rusty-red or chestnut stripe running down the center of the back from head to tail, contrasting with rich brown sides and a grayish belly. The fur feels dense and soft to the touch.

idTips.label: Size & Shape
idTips.description: About 3-4 inches long with a compact, chunky body that feels solid and muscular when handled. The tail is relatively short for a rodent, less than half the body length, and is distinctly bicolored - dark above and light below.

idTips.label: Tracks
idTips.description: Tiny four-toed front prints and five-toed hind prints in snow or soft soil, often in pairs or clusters near logs or vegetation. Tracks are much smaller than a dime and show delicate toe marks.

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Active day and night, often seen scurrying along fallen logs or through leaf litter with quick, jerky movements. Unlike mice, they rarely freeze when startled - instead darting to the nearest cover.

idTips.label: Sign
idTips.description: Small piles of tiny, dark green pellets about the size of rice grains near feeding areas. Look for neat caches of seeds and small gnaw marks on bark, fungi, and berries.

idTips.label: Habitat
idTips.description: Found almost exclusively in cool, moist forests with plenty of fallen logs, mossy rocks, and dense ground cover. They prefer areas with rich leaf litter and decaying wood.

habitat: Southern red-backed voles thrive in cool, moist coniferous and mixed forests throughout New England's mountains and northern regions. They prefer areas with abundant fallen logs, moss-covered rocks, and thick leaf litter that stays damp year-round. You'll find them from sea level to mountain peaks, especially in spruce-fir forests and areas with dense understory vegetation.

seasonality.spring: Active and easier to spot as they search for fresh green vegetation and emerging fungi. This is peak breeding season, so you might see them more frequently during daylight hours.
seasonality.summer: Most active during cooler morning and evening hours, often seen gathering berries and seeds. Their red back stripe is most vibrant during the summer molt.
seasonality.fall: Busy caching seeds, nuts, and dried fungi for winter storage. You'll often find their small food stores under logs or in rock crevices during this season.
seasonality.winter: Remain active under the snow, creating tunnel networks through leaf litter. Look for their tracks in fresh snow leading between tree bases and fallen logs.

funFact: Red-backed voles are nature's little recyclers - they actually eat their own soft droppings to extract every possible nutrient from their food, a process called coprophagy that helps them survive on a diet of tough plant material and fungi.
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with deer mice, but remember 'red back, vole track' - the red stripe is unmistakable, and voles have much shorter tails than mice. Woodland jumping mice also have long tails and lack the red stripe entirely.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'southern' red-backed voles, these are actually northern animals in New England - the name comes from their range being south of other red-backed vole species in Canada and Alaska. They're sometimes found in live-traps meant for other animals, where their calm demeanor makes them easy to identify and release.
compareHints: Since this is the only red-backed vole species in New England, compare it to other small forest rodents like deer mice and woodland voles. Deer mice have white bellies and much longer tails, while woodland voles (pine mice) lack the red back stripe entirely and have even shorter tails. The red back stripe is unique among New England's small mammals.
